arXiv:2504.21776v1 [cs.CL] 30 Apr 2025

WebThinker: Empowering Large Reasoning Models with Deep Research Capability

Xiaoxi Li ††thanks: Equal contribution. Email: xiaoxili@ruc.edu.cn    Jiajie Jin Email: dou@ruc.edu.cn    Guanting Dong    Hongjin Qian    Yutao Zhu    Yongkang Wu Affiliation: Renmin University of China BAAI Huawei Poisson Lab    Ji-Rong Wen    Zhicheng Dou ††thanks: Corresponding author.
Abstract

Large reasoning models (LRMs), such as OpenAI-o1 and DeepSeek-R1, demonstrate impressive long-horizon reasoning capabilities. However, their reliance on static internal knowledge limits their performance on complex, knowledge-intensive tasks and hinders their ability to produce comprehensive research reports requiring synthesis of diverse web information. To address this, we propose WebThinker, a deep research agent that empowers LRMs to autonomously search the web, navigate web pages, and draft research reports during the reasoning process. WebThinker integrates a Deep Web Explorer module, enabling LRMs to dynamically search, navigate, and extract information from the web when encountering knowledge gaps. It also employs an Autonomous Think-Search-and-Draft strategy, allowing the model to seamlessly interleave reasoning, information gathering, and report writing in real time. To further enhance research tool utilization, we introduce an RL-based training strategy via iterative online Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Extensive experiments on complex reasoning benchmarks (GPQA, GAIA, WebWalkerQA, HLE) and scientific report generation tasks (Glaive) demonstrate that WebThinker significantly outperforms existing methods and strong proprietary systems. Our approach enhances LRM reliability and applicability in complex scenarios, paving the way for more capable and versatile deep research systems. The code is available at https://github.com/RUC-NLPIR/WebThinker.

1 Introduction

Recently, large reasoning models (LRMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various domains like math, code, and science [35, 50, 5]. However, when confronted with complex information research needs, models that rely solely on internal knowledge struggle to conduct in-depth web information retrieval and to generate comprehensive and accurate scientific reports through multi-step reasoning. Therefore, the deep integration of LRM’s reasoning capabilities with web information exploration has become a practical demand, which has sparked a series of deep research initiatives by OpenAI [36], xAI Grok3 [14], and Google Gemini [12].

The objective of deep research technology is quite revolutionary: enabling users to conduct deep searches, mining, and integration of comprehensive and reliable research information across the internet’s massive information landscape through simple queries. This approach significantly reduces the time and costs associated with information gathering for researchers in knowledge-intensive fields (e.g., finance, science, engineering).

Unfortunately, existing open-source deep search agents typically employ retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) techniques with predefined workflows [1, 63, 43], which limits LRM’s ability to explore deeper web information and hinders close interaction between LRMs and search engines (Figure 2 (a) & (b)). Consequently, developing a universal, flexible, open-source deep research framework has emerged as a critical challenge urgently awaiting resolution in both academic and industrial circles.

To address this, we propose WebThinker, an open-source deep research agent entirely powered by reasoning models, as illustrated in Figure 2 (c). It enables LRMs to autonomously conduct web searches and web page navigation to acquire external knowledge during the reasoning process, facilitating complex real-world problem solving. Furthermore, WebThinker allows LRMs to draft reports concurrently with thinking and searching. Once sufficient information is gathered for a specific section, the model can draft that part, ultimately producing comprehensive and customized reports tailored to users’ research questions.

To empower LRMs with the capability to deeply explore web information, we design a Deep Web Explorer module that enables LRMs to search, navigate pages by clicking interactive elements (like links or buttons), and extract relevant information. Based on the current query’s search results, the LRM can initiate follow-up searches and traverse deeper links until it collects all relevant information.

To further facilitate scientific report writing, we introduce an Autonomous Think-Search-and-Draft strategy that deeply integrates report writing with the reasoning and search processes of LRMs. Rather than generating the entire report all at once after searching, our approach enables the model to draft and seek necessary knowledge in real-time. To achieve this, we equip LRMs with three specialized tools: (1) drafting content for specific chapters, (2) checking the current report, and (3) editing the report. These tools enable LRMs to autonomously enhance the report by maintaining comprehensiveness, coherence, and adaptability to newly discovered information during reasoning.

To further unlock the deep research potential of LRM backbones, we develop RL-based training strategies to optimize end-to-end task performance. We leverage the LRM equipped with our tools to sample large-scale reasoning trajectories from complex tasks [48, 57, 49, 65, 25]. Using the accuracy of reasoning, tool usage, and final outputs, we construct preference pairs for online DPO training [41, 58, 6]. Through iterative, on-policy training, the model progressively improves its ability to perceive, reason, and interact with research tools effectively.

We conduct extensive experiments on (1) knowledge-intensive complex reasoning benchmarks, including GPQA [42], GAIA [33], WebWalkerQA [57], and Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE) [38] to assess complex problem-solving capabilities, and (2) open-ended reasoning tasks from Glaive [13] to evaluate report quality. As shown in Figure 1, WebThinker consistently outperforms competing approaches on both problem-solving and report generation tasks.

In summary, our core contributions are as follows:

  1. 1.

    We introduce WebThinker, a deep research agent that autonomously search, deeply explore web pages, and draft research reports, all within its thinking process. Unlike traditional predefined workflow, WebThinker enables the LRM itself to perform actions on its own while thinking, achieving end-to-end task execution in a single generation.

  2. 2.

    We propose a Deep Web Explorer that empowers LRMs with web search and navigation capabilities to deeply gather, traverse, and extract high-quality information from the web.

  3. 3.

    We introduce an Autonomous Think-Search-and-Draft strategy that enables real-time report writing during the thinking and searching process.

  4. 4.

    We develop RL-based training strategies that iteratively synthesize tool-usage preference data and apply online DPO training to enhance the LRM’s tool utilization capabilities.

  5. 5.

    We demonstrate the effectiveness of WebThinker on complex reasoning tasks and scientific report generation tasks with both QwQ-based [50] and DeepSeek-R1-based [5] LRM backbones.

2 Related Work

Large Reasoning Models.

Large reasoning models (LRMs) enhance test-time performance through extended reasoning, setting them apart from traditional large pre-trained models that scale mainly with model size or data volume [16, 62, 40, 29, 3]. Models like OpenAI-o1 [21], Qwen-QwQ [50], and DeepSeek-R1 [5] demonstrate explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning [56], resembling human system-2 thinking in tasks such as math and programming [29].

Various strategies have been proposed to achieve o1-like reasoning capabilities [5, 11, 4, 47, 60, 17]. Some approaches introduce intentional reasoning errors during training to help models partially internalize reasoning patterns [39, 64]. Others enhance reasoning ability through distilled training data [34]. More recently, reinforcement learning has been explored as a means to develop long CoT abilities in LLMs [5, 4, 60, 17]. However, these methods are constrained by their reliance on static, parameterized architectures that lack access to external world knowledge. This limitation becomes particularly problematic in complex reasoning tasks requiring extensive real-world information.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances generative models by integrating retrieval mechanisms, enabling access to external knowledge beyond static parameters [24, 66, 28, 68]. Recent advances cover multiple dimensions, including retrieval necessity [46], query reformulation [32, 53], document compression [61, 23, 70], denoising [31, 9], and instruction-following [8, 7, 69]. Moreover, complex workflows such as structured planning [27, 52, 59, 18] and decision-making frameworks [30, 15] have shown notable gains in multi-hop reasoning, planning, and domain-specific tasks [54].

Recent work has also explored integrating o1-style reasoning with retrieval. For example, Search-o1 [26] incorporates an agentic RAG framework and a Reason-in-Documents module to merge retrieval with reasoning via prompt engineering. Other studies employ reinforcement learning to train reasoning with search capabilities from scratch [22, 44, 2, 67, 45], showing strong results in Wikipedia-based QA. Nonetheless, these methods fall short in adapting to complex real-world reasoning scenarios and comprehensive report-writing tasks.

3 Methodology

3.1 Problem Formulation

We consider a complex reasoning task that requires both multi-step reasoning and the utilization of research tools. The objective is to generate a comprehensive solution for a given task query qq, guided by an instruction II. A solution comprises a logical reasoning chain ℛ\mathcal{R} and a final output yy (which could be an answer or a signal indicating completion). WebThinker enables the reasoning model to autonomously invoke tools from an available set 𝒯\mathcal{T} during its reasoning process, which can be formalized as the mapping (I,q,𝒯)→(ℛ,y)(I,q,\mathcal{T})\rightarrow(\mathcal{R},y). The generation process can be expressed as:

P(ℛ,y∣I,q,𝒯)=∏t=1TrP⁡(ℛt∣ℛ<t,I,q,{𝒪τ}τ<t)⏟Reasoning with Tools⋅∏t=1TyP⁡(yt∣y<t,ℛ,I,q)⏟Final Output Generation,P(\mathcal{R},y\mid I,q,\mathcal{T})=\underbrace{\prod\nolimits_{t=1}^{T_{r}}P(\mathcal{R}_{t}\mid\mathcal{R}_{<t},I,q,\{\mathcal{O}_{\tau}\}_{\tau<t})}_{\text{Reasoning with Tools}}\cdot\underbrace{\prod\nolimits_{t=1}^{T_{y}}P(y_{t}\mid y_{<t},\mathcal{R},I,q)}_{\text{Final Output Generation}}, (1)

where TrT_{r} is the number of tokens in the reasoning sequence ℛ\mathcal{R}. The token at position tt is ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t}, and ℛ<t\mathcal{R}_{<t} represents all tokens generated before position tt. {𝒪τ}τ<t\{\mathcal{O}_{\tau}\}_{\tau<t} denotes the outputs of all tool calls made before position tt. Similarly, TyT_{y} is the length of the output sequence yy, with yty_{t} being the token at position tt and y<ty_{<t} indicating all generated output tokens before position tt.

3.2 Overview of the WebThinker Framework

WebThinker is designed to enhance large reasoning models with deep research capabilities by enabling autonomous web exploration and report generation during the reasoning process. As illustrated in Figure 3, WebThinker operates in two primary modes:

  • •

    Problem-Solving Mode: Empowers the LRM with a Deep Web Explorer module. When encountering knowledge gaps, the LRM can autonomously initiate web searches, navigate through web pages by clicking links or buttons, and extract relevant information before continuing its reasoning. This facilitates in-depth information gathering beyond standard shallow search.

  • •

    Report Generation Mode: Implements an Autonomous Think-Search-and-Draft strategy. The LRM can interleave reasoning, information seeking (via the Deep Web Explorer), and report composition. It utilizes specialized tools for drafting, checking, and editing report sections, managed by an assistant LLM, ensuring the final report is comprehensive, coherent, and grounded in the gathered evidence.

The subsequent sections provide details of these components and the RL-based training strategies.

3.3 Solving Complex Reasoning Tasks with the Deep Web Explorer

In the Problem-Solving Mode, WebThinker tackles complex tasks requiring knowledge beyond the LRM’s internal parameters. The core component is the Deep Web Explorer tool, 𝒯exp∈𝒯\mathcal{T}_{\text{exp}}\in\mathcal{T}, which the LRM can invoke during reasoning (Figure 3).

Given a task-specific instruction IqI_{q} and query qq, the LRM generates a reasoning chain ℛ\mathcal{R}, potentially interspersed with calls to the Deep Web Explorer. The final output in this mode is typically a direct answer aa. The generation process is formalized as:

P(ℛ,a∣Iq,q)=∏t=1TrP(ℛt∣ℛ<t,Iq,q,{𝒪exp(j)}j<i⁡(t))⋅∏t=1TaP(at∣a<t,ℛ,Iq,q),P(\mathcal{R},a\mid I_{q},q)=\prod\nolimits_{t=1}^{T_{r}}P(\mathcal{R}_{t}\mid\mathcal{R}_{<t},I_{q},q,\{\mathcal{O}_{\text{exp}}^{(j)}\}_{j<i(t)})\cdot\prod\nolimits_{t=1}^{T_{a}}P(a_{t}\mid a_{<t},\mathcal{R},I_{q},q), (2)

where a=(a1,…,aTa)a=(a_{1},\dots,a_{T_{a}}) is the answer sequence. {𝒪exp(j)}j<i⁡(t)\{\mathcal{O}_{\text{exp}}^{(j)}\}_{j<i(t)} denotes the set of outputs from all Deep Web Explorer calls completed prior to reasoning step tt.

The Deep Web Explorer itself is driven by the LRM, operating under a specific instruction IeI_{e}. It utilizes two elementary tools: a search engine 𝒯s\mathcal{T}_{\text{s}} to retrieve web pages based on a generated query qsq_{\text{s}}, and a navigation tool 𝒯n\mathcal{T}_{\text{n}} to interact with elements (e.g., click links) on the currently viewed page(s) 𝒟\mathcal{D}. The explorer, triggered by an information need qsq_{\text{s}}, generates its own internal reasoning chain ℛe\mathcal{R}_{\text{e}} to decide whether to search further or navigate deeper based on the evolving web content 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} it encounters. Its goal is to produce a concise output 𝒪exp\mathcal{O}_{\text{exp}} that addresses the knowledge gap in the main reasoning chain ℛ\mathcal{R}. The exploration process within the tool is modeled as:

P(ℛe,𝒪exp∣qs,𝒟,Ie)=∏t=1TeP(ℛe,t∣ℛe,<t,qs,𝒟t,Ie)⋅P(𝒪exp∣ℛe,qs,𝒟,Ie),P(\mathcal{R}_{\text{e}},\mathcal{O}_{\text{exp}}\mid q_{\text{s}},\mathcal{D},I_{e})=\prod\nolimits_{t=1}^{T_{e}}P(\mathcal{R}_{\text{e},t}\mid\mathcal{R}_{\text{e},<t},q_{\text{s}},\mathcal{D}_{t},I_{e})\cdot P(\mathcal{O}_{\text{exp}}\mid\mathcal{R}_{\text{e}},q_{\text{s}},\mathcal{D},I_{e}), (3)

where TeT_{e} is the length of the explorer’s reasoning chain ℛe\mathcal{R}_{\text{e}}. 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} represents the web content available at step tt, which dynamically changes based on search and navigation actions. This hierarchical structure allows the main reasoning process to delegate complex information gathering tasks to the Deep Web Explorer, which can recursively search and navigate the web.

3.4 Generating Comprehensive Reports via Autonomous Think-Search-and-Draft

In the Report Generation Mode, the LRM autonomously produces comprehensive reports by interleaving reasoning, searching, and writing. Besides the Deep Web Explorer (𝒯exp\mathcal{T}_{\text{exp}}) for knowledge acquisition, the LRM utilizes a set of report writing tools 𝒯write={𝒯draft,𝒯check,𝒯edit}\mathcal{T}_{\text{write}}=\{\mathcal{T}_{\text{draft}},\mathcal{T}_{\text{check}},\mathcal{T}_{\text{edit}}\}. These tools are implemented by an assistant LLM, separating the complex task orchestration performed by the main LRM from the detailed text manipulation required for report writing.

All web pages explored via 𝒯exp\mathcal{T}_{\text{exp}} are accumulated in a document memory ℳ\mathcal{M}. When the main LRM decides to invoke a writing tool (e.g., 𝒯draft\mathcal{T}_{\text{draft}}), it generates an editing instruction ee. The assistant model then receives ee, the current report state rr, and relevant documents 𝒟top-k\mathcal{D}_{\text{top-k}} retrieved from ℳ\mathcal{M}. It produces the updated report content rnewr_{\text{new}} according to:

P⁡(rnew∣e,𝒟top-k,r)=∏t=1TrnewP⁡(rnew,t∣rnew,<t,e,𝒟top-k,r),P(r_{\text{new}}\mid e,\mathcal{D}_{\text{top-k}},r)=\prod\nolimits_{t=1}^{T_{r_{\text{new}}}}P(r_{\text{new},t}\mid r_{\text{new},<t},e,\mathcal{D}_{\text{top-k}},r), (4)

where TrnewT_{r_{\text{new}}} is the length of the newly generated/edited report content rnewr_{\text{new}}.

The main LRM’s role is to orchestrate the overall process: performing reasoning steps, deciding when to explore for more information using 𝒯exp\mathcal{T}_{\text{exp}}, and determining when and how to modify the report using 𝒯write\mathcal{T}_{\text{write}}. The main reasoning process concludes when the LRM generates the EOS token, denoted as yendy_{\text{end}}. This overall process, conditioned on the initial instruction II and query qq, is formalized as:

P(ℛ,yend∣I,q)=∏t=1TrP(ℛt∣ℛ<t,I,q,{𝒪exp(j)}j<i⁡(t))⋅P(yend∣ℛ,ℳ),P(\mathcal{R},y_{\text{end}}\mid I,q)=\prod\nolimits_{t=1}^{T_{r}}P(\mathcal{R}_{t}\mid\mathcal{R}_{<t},I,q,\{\mathcal{O}_{\text{exp}}^{(j)}\}_{j<i(t)})\cdot P(y_{\text{end}}\mid\mathcal{R},\mathcal{M}), (5)

where {𝒪exp(j)}j<i⁡(t)\{\mathcal{O}_{\text{exp}}^{(j)}\}_{j<i(t)} represents outputs from prior Deep Web Explorer calls. Although the report state rr is not directly input to the main LRM’s generation step (Eq. 5), the LRM implicitly tracks progress and uses tools based on the research status reflected in the reasoning chain ℛ\mathcal{R} and potentially available context. The document memory ℳ\mathcal{M} serves as the knowledge base for the assistant LLM (Eq. 4) executing the writing operations.

This iterative design allows the main LRM to maintain high-level control over research direction and report structure, while the assistant LLM handles the detailed writing, ensuring the final report is well-supported by evidence from ℳ\mathcal{M}.

3.5 Improving LRMs with Research Tools via Reinforcement Learning

To enhance the LRM’s ability to effectively utilize research tools that range from high-level web exploration and report manipulation to elementary search and navigation actions, we employ on-policy RL training. This focuses on constructing preference data reflecting desired tool usage patterns and applying an iterative online DPO [41, 58, 6] strategy.

Preference Data Construction.

We generate diverse reasoning trajectories by applying the WebThinker framework to a comprehensive set of complex reasoning and report generation datasets: SuperGPQA [48], WebWalkerQA [57], OpenThoughts [49], NaturalReasoning [65], NuminaMath [25] and Glaive [13]. For each query qq, our initial LRM produces nn distinct trajectories {ℛ(i)}i=1n\{\mathcal{R}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{n}. This self-sampling approach explores varied solution strategies, capturing different tool usage patterns across both the main reasoning chain and the Deep Web Explorer’s internal reasoning process.

Our goal is to identify trajectories that demonstrate not only correctness but also efficient use of the research tools. To achieve this, we establish preference pairs (ℛw,ℛl)(\mathcal{R}_{w},\mathcal{R}_{l}), where ℛw\mathcal{R}_{w} is the preferred trajectory and ℛl\mathcal{R}_{l} is the dis-preferred trajectory. We apply the following criteria iteratively in order of priority to pairs of sampled trajectories (ℛi,ℛj)(\mathcal{R}_{i},\mathcal{R}_{j}) for the same task qq:

  1. 1.

    Overall Correctness/Quality: If ℛi\mathcal{R}_{i} yields a correct final answer (for reasoning tasks) or a higher quality final report (for report generation tasks), while ℛj\mathcal{R}_{j} does not, then ℛi\mathcal{R}_{i} is preferred (ℛw=ℛi,ℛl=ℛj\mathcal{R}_{w}=\mathcal{R}_{i},\mathcal{R}_{l}=\mathcal{R}_{j}). This rule takes precedence over all others.

  2. 2.

    Tool Efficiency: If both ℛi\mathcal{R}_{i} and ℛj\mathcal{R}_{j} reach the correct final answer, the trajectory with fewer total tool calls is preferred. If total_tool_calls​(ℛi)<total_tool_calls​(ℛj)\text{total\_tool\_calls}(\mathcal{R}_{i})<\text{total\_tool\_calls}(\mathcal{R}_{j}), then ℛw=ℛi,ℛl=ℛj\mathcal{R}_{w}=\mathcal{R}_{i},\mathcal{R}_{l}=\mathcal{R}_{j}.

  3. 3.

    Thinking Conciseness: If both ℛi\mathcal{R}_{i} and ℛj\mathcal{R}_{j} are correct and involve the same number of tool calls, the shorter trajectory is preferred when the length ratio exceeds the threshold γ>1\gamma>1. If len​(outputj)/len​(outputi)>γ\text{len}(\text{output}_{j})/\text{len}(\text{output}_{i})>\gamma, then ℛw=ℛi,ℛl=ℛj\mathcal{R}_{w}=\mathcal{R}_{i},\mathcal{R}_{l}=\mathcal{R}_{j}.

By applying these rules across all valid sampled trajectory pairs for all tasks, we construct a collection 𝒟={(I,q,ℛw,ℛl)k}\mathcal{D}=\{(I,q,\mathcal{R}_{w},\mathcal{R}_{l})_{k}\} of preference pairs.

Iterative Online DPO Training.

We utilize the constructed preference dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} to train the LRM using iterative online DPO. The standard DPO loss function aims to increase the likelihood of preferred trajectories ℛw\mathcal{R}_{w} while decreasing the likelihood of dispreferred trajectories ℛl\mathcal{R}_{l}, relative to a reference policy πref\pi_{\text{ref}}:

ℒDPO​(πθ,πref)=−𝔼(ℛw,ℛl)∼𝒟​[log⁡σ⁡(β​log⁡πθ​(ℛw∣I,q)πref​(ℛw∣I,q)−β​log⁡πθ​(ℛl∣I,q)πref​(ℛl∣I,q))],\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}(\pi_{\theta};\pi_{\text{ref}})=-\mathbb{E}_{(\mathcal{R}_{w},\mathcal{R}_{l})\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\log\sigma\left(\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(\mathcal{R}_{w}\mid I,q)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(\mathcal{R}_{w}\mid I,q)}-\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(\mathcal{R}_{l}\mid I,q)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(\mathcal{R}_{l}\mid I,q)}\right)\right], (6)

where πθ\pi_{\theta} is the policy being trained, β\beta is a hyperparameter controlling the deviation from the reference policy, and σ\sigma is the sigmoid function.

We employ an iterative online scheme: (1) Train πθ\pi_{\theta} on the current preference set 𝒟\mathcal{D} using Eq. 6. (2) Use the updated πθ\pi_{\theta} to sample new trajectories for the tasks (exploration). (3) Apply the preference criteria (1-3) to the new trajectories to generate an updated preference set 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime}. (4) Set 𝒟←𝒟′\mathcal{D}\leftarrow\mathcal{D}^{\prime} and πref←πθ\pi_{\text{ref}}\leftarrow\pi_{\theta}, then repeat from step (1). This iterative loop allows the LRM to learn from online feedback generated by its own improving policy, progressively refining its complex tool usage strategy through interaction with the task environment in an on-policy fashion.

4 Experiments

4.1 Tasks and Datasets

We evaluate WebThinker on two primary task categories:

Complex Reasoning Benchmarks: Assesses the model’s ability to solve intricate problems requiring multi-step reasoning and external knowledge. We utilize several benchmarks: GPQA [42], a PhD-level science question answering dataset covering physics, chemistry, and biology (we use the diamond set comprising 198 questions); GAIA [33], a benchmark designed to evaluate general AI assistants on complex information retrieval tasks (we use 103 questions from the text-only validation subset); WebWalkerQA [57], a dataset focused on deep web information retrieval, requiring navigation and extraction (we use the test set containing 680 questions); and Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE) [38], an extremely challenging dataset featuring problems across various disciplines (mathematics, biology, physics, computer science, etc.) that demand advanced search and reasoning skills (we sampled 500 questions from its text-only subset for experimental efficiency). Accuracy for these tasks is judged by Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct [40].

Scientific Report Generation Tasks: Evaluates the model’s capability to synthesize comprehensive research reports for open-ended questions. We use glaiveai/reasoning-v1-20m (Glaive) [13], a large-scale dataset of general, open-ended reasoning questions covering a wide range of subjects, suitable for evaluating research capabilities across various aspects. We sample 30 diverse questions from this dataset as our test set. Reports are evaluated using average scores judged by DeepSeek-R1-671B [5] and GPT-4o [20]. All data used in our experiments can be found in our GitHub repository11 1 https://github.com/RUC-NLPIR/WebThinker/tree/main/data.

4.2 Baselines

We compare WebThinker against several baseline methods:

Direct Reasoning: Models using only internal knowledge without retrieval. Includes open-source models (Qwen2.5-32B/72B-Instruct [40], Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct [19], QwQ-32B [50], Llama3.3-70B-Instruct [10]) and closed-source models (DeepSeek-R1-671B [5], GPT-4o [20], o1-preview [35], o3-mini [37], Gemini-2.0-Flash-Thinking [12]).

Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning: Methods using external knowledge from search engines. We test three variants: (1) Standard RAG, retrieving top-10 documents for the original query before generation; (2) RAG w/ Query Planning, decomposing the query into sub-queries, retrieving for each, then generating; and (3) Iterative RAG, which iteratively retrieves information, deciding whether to search further or generate the final answer.

Autonomous Search within Reasoning: Systems integrating search actions into the reasoning process. Includes the open-source Search-o1 framework [26] and non-proprietary systems like OpenAI Deep Research [36], Grok3 DeeperSearch [14], and Gemini2.0 Deep Research [12].

4.3 Implementation Details

For the backbone reasoning model for WebThinker, we utilize the open-source QwQ-32B [50] in our main results and DeepSeek-R1-Distilled-Qwen-[7B, 14B, 32B] [5] in Figure 5. For assistant models, we use Qwen2.5-Instruct [40] with the same parameters as the backbone LRM. For generation, we use a maximum of 81920 tokens, temperature of 0.7, top_p of 0.8, top_k of 20, and a repetition penalty of 1.05 across all models. For search, we use the Bing Web Search API, configured for the US-EN region, retrieving the top 10 search results (k=10). Web page content corresponding to the retrieved URLs is fetched using Crawl4AI [51]. Model training consists of 2 iterations of online DPO with a maximum sequence length of 32768. For baseline models not specifically trained for o1-like reasoning, we employ Chain-of-Thought (CoT) [56] prompting to guide the reasoning process prior to answer generation. Detailed instructions for all models are provided in Appendix C. All experiments are conducted on 4 nodes of 8 NVIDIA H100-80GB GPUs.

4.4 Results on Complex Problem-Solving

Main Results.

Tables 1 and 2 present WebThinker’s performance on complex reasoning tasks. Key findings include:

  1. 1.

    Limitations of Base LRMs and RAG Workflow: While reasoning models like QwQ-32B outperform standard LLMs (e.g., Qwen2.5-72B on GPQA avg.), their direct reasoning capabilities struggle on knowledge-intensive tasks like GAIA and WebWalkerQA. Although RAG workflows improve performance on these tasks, they fail to show consistent gains on complex HLE tasks due to challenges in integrating with deep reasoning.

  2. 2.

    Autonomous Search Advantage: Incorporating autonomous search within reasoning, as demonstrated by Search-o1, provides notable gains over direct reasoning and basic RAG, particularly on GAIA, WebWalkerQA, and HLE (e.g., Search-o1 avg. 10.8 vs. RAG-QwQ-32B avg. 7.2 on HLE).

  3. 3.

    Superiority of the WebThinker Framework: Our WebThinker framework further enhances performance. The WebThinker-32B-Base model, utilizing the Deep Web Explorer to deepen web exploration, consistently surpasses prior methods like Search-o1 across all benchmarks (e.g., 22.9% and 20.4% improvement on WebWalkerQA and HLE, respectively).

  4. 4.

    RL Improvement: The WebThinker-32B-RL model, refined through our RL-based training, achieves state-of-the-art results among 32B models on all tested benchmarks. It demonstrates substantial improvements over the Base version (e.g., 8.5% and 21.5% improvement on GAIA and HLE, respectively). Notably, on the challenging HLE benchmark, WebThinker-32B-RL surpasses even the performance of stronger models like o3-mini (High).

4.5 Results on Scientific Report Generation

Main Results.

Figure 4 (left) shows the performance of WebThinker compared to baselines (RAG and non-proprietary systems) on the Glaive scientific report generation task. Performance is evaluated by DeepSeek-R1 and GPT-4o across Completeness (Comp.), Thoroughness (Thorough.), Factuality (Fact.), and Coherence. WebThinker achieves the highest overall score (8.0), outperforming both RAG baselines and advanced deep research systems such as Gemini-Deep Research (7.9). It particularly excels in Completeness (8.4) and Thoroughness (8.2), while matching the top scores in Factuality (7.7) and Coherence (7.8). These results underscore the effectiveness of the Autonomous Think-Search-and-Draft strategy, which fully unlocks LRM’s capabilities to iteratively refine content through dynamic information gathering, resulting in more comprehensive and coherent reports than approaches limited by predefined RAG workflows.

Analysis of Information Scopes.

To qualitatively assess the generated reports, we visualize their content embeddings using t-SNE for three randomly sampled topics from the Glaive dataset (Figure 4, right). Each point corresponds to the embedding of a report generated by one of the compared methods. The visualization reveals distinct clusters for each topic, confirming that all methods produce topic-specific content. Notably, reports generated by WebThinker often form broader sub-clusters within each topic group. This suggests that WebThinker, leveraging its Deep Web Explorer and iterative drafting process, explores and synthesizes information from diverse perspectives and depths compared to other methods. Its autonomous nature enables it to adapt the information gathering and writing process dynamically to the report’s evolving requirements, leading to richer and potentially more unique information coverage.

4.6 Adaptability of WebThinker Across Different LRM Backbones.

To evaluate WebThinker’s adaptability across different LRM backbones, we experimented with DeepSeek-R1 models of varying sizes (7B, 14B, and 32B), as illustrated in Figure 5. To ensure stable tool usage capabilities in the R1-based LRMs, we first conducted cold-start supervised fine-tuning (SFT) using 7.8k reasoning trajectories collected from the QwQ-32B-based WebThinker, followed by reinforcement learning (RL) training (Section 3.5). Across all model sizes and tasks (GAIA, WebWalkerQA, HLE, Glaive), the R1-based WebThinker models consistently outperformed direct reasoning and standard RAG baselines. For example, with the DeepSeek-R1-7B backbone, WebThinker achieves relative improvements of 174.4% on GAIA and 422.6% on WebWalkerQA over direct generation, and 82.9% on GAIA and 161.3% on WebWalkerQA over standard RAG. Similar substantial gains are observed across other model sizes and tasks. These results demonstrate the general applicability and strong effectiveness of the WebThinker framework in enhancing the deep research capabilities of diverse LRMs.

4.7 Ablation Studies

We conducted ablation studies to evaluate the contribution of key WebThinker components, with results summarized in Table 3. (1) Impact of RL Training: Iterative online RL significantly enhances problem-solving performance (Avg. 44.9 vs. 42.1 for the base model and 43.2 for offline DPO), validating the efficacy of the training strategy. However, its impact on report generation is minimal, indicating that the base framework is already highly effective. (2) Importance of Deep Web Exploration: Removing the Deep Web Explorer drastically reduces performance in both problem-solving (Avg. 38.3) and report generation (Avg. 7.7), highlighting its critical role. Additionally, disabling only link-clicking negatively impacts problem-solving (Avg. 42.6), demonstrating the value of exploring beyond initial search results, especially for navigation-intensive tasks. (3) Effectiveness of Report Generation Components: For report generation, removing autonomous drafting results in the most significant quality drop (Avg. 6.6), underscoring the importance of interleaving thinking, searching, and drafting. Similarly, disabling the check-and-edit tools lowers overall quality (Avg. 7.7), particularly coherence (6.9 vs. 7.9), reinforcing the necessity of iterative refinement. These results affirm the effectiveness of WebThinker’s design choices.

5 Conclusion

In this work, we present WebThinker, a framework that equips large reasoning models (LRMs) with deep research capabilities, addressing their limitations in knowledge-intensive real-world tasks such as complex reasoning and scientific report generation. WebThinker enables LRMs to autonomously explore the web and produce comprehensive outputs through a continuous reasoning process. Key contributions include the Deep Web Explorer, which empowers LRMs to dynamically search and navigate web content, and the Autonomous Think-Search-and-Draft strategy, which seamlessly integrates reasoning, searching, and report writing. In addition, we introduce RL-based training strategies that further refine the LRM’s ability to effectively utilize research tools. Extensive experiments on complex reasoning benchmarks and scientific report generation tasks demonstrate that WebThinker consistently outperforms existing methods and even strong proprietary systems. These findings underscore WebThinker’s potential to significantly advance the deep research capabilities of LRMs, paving the way for more powerful and versatile intelligent systems capable of addressing complex real-world challenges.

Looking ahead, we plan to extend WebThinker in several directions. First, we aim to incorporate multimodal reasoning capabilities, enabling deep research involving images, videos, and other non-textual information and leveraging the rich multimodal content available online. Second, we will explore advanced tool learning and expansion mechanisms, allowing WebThinker to continuously refine its tool usage strategies through self-improvement and to integrate a broader range of external tools. Finally, we intend to investigate GUI-based web exploration, enhancing the model’s ability to understand and interact with graphical web interfaces and enabling it to tackle more complex interactive tasks.

Appendix

Appendix A Inference Process

A.1 Research-Related Tools

WebThinker utilizes several tools during its inference process:

  • •

    Search Tool: This tool is employed by both the main reasoning process and the Deep Web Explorer. In the main process, it invokes the Deep Web Explorer, while within the Explorer, it calls a standard search engine API. The model signals a search query by generating and . The processed search results are then returned within and .

  • •

    Link & Button Clicking Tool: This tool is exclusively used by the Deep Web Explorer to interact with web pages, typically invoking a web crawler. We use Crawl4AI [51] for fetching web page content. The model triggers this tool by generating and . The content retrieved from the clicked link (potentially summarized) is returned within and .

  • •

    Report Writing Tools: These tools are specific to the Report Generation Mode and are invoked by the main reasoning process. They facilitate drafting and refining the research report.

    • –

      Section Writing: Triggered by section_name\ncontents_to_write . This command instructs an assistant LLM to write the specified section based on the provided content guidelines and gathered information. It does not return content directly into the main reasoning flow to maintain coherence.

    • –

      Report Checking: Triggered by . This command requests the current outline of the report. The system extracts all section and subsection titles to form the outline, which is then inserted into the reasoning context followed by . This avoids injecting the full report text, which could disrupt the reasoning flow.

    • –

      Report Editing: Triggered by edit_instruction . This command instructs an assistant LLM to modify the existing report based on the provided editing instructions. Similar to section writing, it doesn’t return content directly into the main flow.

A.2 Inference Process of WebThinker

The overall inference process in WebThinker involves two main components: the main reasoning process and the Deep Web Explorer for in-depth information gathering. As outlined in Section 3.2, the main reasoning process operates in two distinct modes: Problem-Solving Mode and Report Generation Mode. Detailed instructions for each component and mode can be found in Section C.

A.2.1 Inference for Main Reasoning Process

Problem-Solving Mode:

In this mode, the LRM receives a user’s question and aims to find a direct answer. It primarily utilizes the Search Tool. When the model generates the token, the generation process pauses. The system extracts the most recent query enclosed within and . Concurrently, an assistant LLM formulates a detailed search intent based on the query and the preceding reasoning chain. The system then uses a web crawler to fetch the content of the top-k (k=10 in our experiments) retrieved web documents. The original query, the generated search intent, and the fetched web content are passed to the Deep Web Explorer. The Explorer processes this information and returns a refined summary relevant to the query and intent, enclosed within and . The main LRM then resumes its reasoning with this new information. This cycle continues until the model generates an End-of-Sequence (EOS) token or reaches the maximum token limit. The final answer is extracted based on a predefined answer pattern (e.g., \boxed{ANSWER} or ANSWER: {ANSWER}).

Report Generation Mode:

This mode handles tasks requiring the generation of a comprehensive research report. It receives the user’s question along with a research plan (potentially generated by an assistant LLM). The LRM utilizes the Search Tool (invoking the Deep Web Explorer as in Problem-Solving Mode) and the three Report Writing Tools (Section Writing, Report Checking, Report Editing). Similar to the problem-solving mode, generation pauses whenever the model outputs a closing tool token (, , ) or the opening token for checking ().

  • •

    For search, the process mirrors the Problem-Solving Mode: invoke the Deep Web Explorer and insert results between and .

  • •

    For section writing and report editing, the corresponding assistant LLM performs the action in the background. Since no direct output is inserted, the main LRM continues its reasoning immediately after generating the end token.

  • •

    For report checking, the system generates the report outline, appends the token, inserts this into the context, and resumes generation.

The model continues this loop of reasoning, searching, and drafting/editing until it generates an EOS token or reaches the maximum token limit. The final, complete report is the accumulated result of the writing and editing actions performed by the assistant LLM throughout the process.

A.2.2 Inference for Deep Web Explorer

Deep Web Explorer:

The Deep Web Explorer operates as a sub-process invoked by the main reasoning process when a search is needed. Its goal is to deeply investigate the initial search results provided by the main process. It has access to two tools: a direct Search Engine call and the Link & Button Clicking Tool. When the Explorer model generates or , generation pauses.

  • •

    A search action directly calls the search engine API (e.g., Bing) and returns the top-10 results, typically including titles, URLs, and snippets (not the full page content). These results are inserted into the Explorer’s reasoning context.

  • •

    A link click action uses the crawler (Crawl4AI) to fetch the full content of the specified URL. To manage potentially long web pages, an assistant LLM summarizes the fetched content based on a generated "click intent", ensuring the inserted information is concise and relevant. The summarized result is placed within and .

The Explorer continues its internal reasoning process—analyzing results, deciding whether to perform another search, or clicking on a promising link—until it gathers sufficient information relevant to the initial query and search intent provided by the main reasoning process. It concludes by generating its findings within a designated "Final Information" pattern, which is then passed back to the main reasoning process as the output within and . This process stops when the Explorer generates an EOS token or reaches its maximum token limit.

Appendix B Datasets

B.1 Complex Reasoning Tasks

For testing, we use the following four widely used datasets:

  • •

    GPQA [42]: Written by experts (holding or pursuing PhDs in relevant fields) in biology, physics, and chemistry, these "Google-proof" questions test the model’s expertise and reasoning in these specific domains. It consists of multiple-choice questions (4 options each); we use the diamond set, totaling 198 questions.

  • •

    GAIA [33]: A benchmark dataset designed to evaluate the capabilities of general artificial intelligence (AGI). Compared to GPQA, GAIA focuses more on generality, testing AI performance across diverse tasks such as question answering, reasoning, code generation, and multimodal processing. As our model is text-based and cannot handle other modalities, we use the text-only validation subset, comprising 103 questions.

  • •

    WebWalkerQA [57]: A benchmark specifically designed to evaluate the web traversal capabilities of LLMs, simulating human ability to explore websites via clicking to find required information. It includes 680 challenging queries covering multilingual and multi-domain web content. We use the test set for evaluation, totaling 680 questions.

  • •

    Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE) [38]: Aims to assess LLMs’ capabilities at the frontiers of human knowledge. It contains 2500 challenging cross-disciplinary questions covering fields like mathematics, humanities, and natural sciences. The benchmark includes multiple-choice and short-answer questions, all with clear and easily verifiable solutions. Current state-of-the-art models achieve less than 10% accuracy on HLE, highlighting its difficulty and effectiveness in measuring advanced academic capabilities. Due to its large test set, we randomly sample 500 text-only questions for testing.

For training, we use the following datasets. We sample approximately 3k data points from these datasets. First, we perform direct generation using QwQ-32B and retain only the questions that cannot be answered correctly through direct generation. Then, for each of these questions, we generate three responses using WebThinker-32B-Base to filter for high-quality preference training data, following the criteria outlined in Section 3.5.

  • •

    SuperGPQA [48]: Designed to evaluate LLM knowledge and reasoning across 285 graduate-level subjects. It contains 26,529 multiple-choice questions covering 72 fields, grouped into 13 broader disciplines, with a strong emphasis on STEM subjects (77.2%).

  • •

    WebWalkerQA (Silver) [57]: We use the Silver set of WebWalkerQA, containing 13.6k data points. The description is the same as above.

  • •

    OpenThoughts [49]: Contains 114,000 carefully crafted reasoning examples designed to train AI models for complex logical and mathematical reasoning tasks. Given that we already use NuminaMath as training data, we prioritize sampling data related to STEM and puzzles.

  • •

    NaturalReasoning [65]: Aims to enhance LLM reasoning capabilities through 2.8 million challenging reasoning problems across multiple domains, including STEM (e.g., physics and computer science), economics, and social sciences.

  • •

    NuminaMath [25]: Features problems ranging in difficulty from high school exercises to International Mathematical Olympiad questions, sourced from various online platforms and PDFs. NuminaMath provides high-quality, structured data enabling AI models to learn and replicate expert-level mathematical reasoning.

B.2 Scientific Report Generation Tasks

For the scientific report generation task, we use glaiveai/reasoning-v1-20m (Glaive) [13] for both training and testing. This dataset is a large-scale synthetic collection containing over 22 million general reasoning questions and responses generated using DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B [5].

It aims to cover diverse non-code/math topics such as social and natural sciences, education, and creative writing. We sample 1.5k questions for each iteration’s preference data construction and 30 questions for testing.

C.2 Task Instructions

The task instruction specifies the description of a specific task and the answer output format for a particular model. These instructions are directly concatenated after the method instructions (such as those for WebThinker, Search-o1, or RAG approaches).

C.2.1 Task Instruction for QwQ-based Models

C.2.2 Task Instruction for DeepSeek-R1-based Models

C.3 Instructions for Evaluation

In this work, we use LLM-as-Judges to evaluate both complex problem-solving and scientific report generation tasks. The specific instructions are as follows:

C.3.1 Evaluation Instruction for Problem-Solving Tasks

We use Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct [40] to evaluate all complex problem-solving tasks. An output labeled as "Correct" is considered correct, while "Incorrect" is considered wrong. In cases where the predicted answer cannot be accurately extracted, we directly use the last five lines of the model’s output as the predicted answer. This approach helps reduce evaluation inaccuracies caused by formatting issues, case sensitivity, and similar factors, aligning with the official evaluation methods of benchmarks like WebWalkerQA [57] and HLE [38].

C.3.2 Evaluation Instruction for Report Quality

For scientific report generation tasks, we use DeepSeek-R1-671B [5] and GPT-4o [20] respectively with the following instruction for evaluation, obtain scores, and take their average. Here, {system_a} to {system_e} are sequentially the reports generated by the systems being evaluated. We perform listwise evaluation to better compare the quality differences between reports generated by different systems. The input order is randomized rather than fixed to reduce bias caused by the model’s context window. We did not employ human evaluation because the reports generated by each system have distinct features, making it easy for humans to identify their originating system, which introduces significant bias. Model-based evaluation is therefore more impartial.

C.4 Additional Notes

All instructions presented above are provided as user prompts rather than system prompts. When applying the WebThinker approach (detailed in Section C.1) to models based on QwQ-32B [50] or DeepSeek-R1 series [5], the corresponding task instruction (from Section C.2.1 or C.2.2) is appended after the main WebThinker instruction. For other models, such as Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct [40], Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct [40], and GPT-4o [20], we include the Chain-of-Thought prompt "You should think step by step to solve it." before the question to explicitly encourage step-by-step reasoning prior to providing the final answer, following [55].

For detailed instructions regarding the baseline methods like Search-o1, Standard RAG, etc., you can refer to the appendix of Search-o1 [26] or visit our WebThinker GitHub repository: https://github.com/sunnynexus/WebThinker.

Appendix D Case Study

The examples from Tables 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10 demonstrate WebThinker’s effectiveness across different capabilities including complex problem solving, deep web exploration, and scientific report generation.

D.1 Case Study for Complex Problem Solving

WebThinker shows strong reasoning capabilities in complex problem-solving scenarios:

  • •

    In the GAIA dataset example (Table 4), WebThinker correctly identifies that Nemo from "Finding Nemo" is a clownfish, and methodically searches for nonnative sightings in the USGS database, finding the only documented case at Fred Howard Park, Florida. It then determines the correct zip code (34689).

  • •

    For the WebWalkerQA example (Table 5), WebThinker resolves ambiguity about the "evening after" the ACL 2023 awards ceremony by searching for relevant dates and determining that the social event occurred on the same day (July 11) from 7:00 PM to 10:30 PM, not the following day.

  • •

    In the mathematical problem from Humanity’s Last Exam (Table 6), WebThinker demonstrates sophisticated reasoning by finding the formula for simplicial volume of surfaces and their products, correctly calculating the simplicial volume of Σ31×Σ17\Sigma_{31}\times\Sigma_{17} as 11520.

D.2 Case Study for Deep Web Explorer

The Deep Web Explorer demonstrates effective information retrieval and integration:

  • •

    For the ASH Annual Meeting deadlines (Table 7), the explorer not only finds the late-breaking abstract submission dates but also discovers the ancillary meeting deadline by clicking on a PDF link, compiling comprehensive deadline information with specific dates and requirements.

  • •

    In the CLTS and Aedes mosquito control example (Table 8), the explorer clicks on a repository link to find a case study integrating Community-Led Total Sanitation with mosquito control in Indonesia, Vietnam, and the Philippines, providing specific outcomes (40% reduction in breeding sites).

D.3 Case Study for Scientific Report Generation

WebThinker’s report generation capability is illustrated in Tables 9 and 10:

  • •

    The model systematically follows a research plan for optimizing 3D printed lattice structures, conducting searches on FDM limitations, lattice optimization techniques, and material properties.

  • •

    It methodically writes, checks, and edits sections, addressing duplicate content and ensuring coherent structure.

  • •

    The final report (Table 10) presents a comprehensive analysis of lattice optimization for robotic nodes, covering technical aspects from printing limitations to material selection, with practical applications and case studies.

These examples validate WebThinker’s effectiveness across complex problem-solving, deep web exploration, and scientific report generation tasks.
